7.2.2. Votive Inscriptions

 

Two Sumerian inscriptions, which deal with the offering of ex-voto
obj to gods, yield new information about the number of wives
and children in a family. One text of the Pre-Sargonic period '!3
names the votant, his wife, and eight children. The votant is a barber
by profession or occupation. The sex of his children is not apparent
from the Sumerian names they bear. The other text, from the Sargonic
period ''*, names the votant, who is a city scribe, his wife, and at
least eight children, of whom — to judge by their Sumerian names

 

 

 

 

at least four are male and four are female.

According to these two inscriptions, each family was monogamous
and it contained a larger than usual number of children. One has to
remember, however, that votive offerings were made by rather pros-
perous individuals, and the two families represented in the votive
inscriptions may have therefore occupied a higher than average

economic status.

 

Royal Family

We pass on to the consideration of the royal family. At first, the
structure of the royal family appears consistent with what we have
learned about the non-royal family from the two votive inscriptions.

By the time of the Ur III dynasty, we are faced with problems relating
to the number of wives and children

The so-called “family bas-reliefs” of Ur-Nanse, ruler of Lagash
in the Pre-Sargonic period ''®, show the representations and give the
names of his wife, seven or eight children, and of other individuals,
one of whom is a senior snake charmer, the other a scribe.

W.W. Hallo lists five children of Sargon and eight children of
Narfm-Sin in the Sargonic period ''®. He names one wife for each
of the five kings of the Third Dynasty of Ur and as many as 20
children of Sulgi!'7.

E. Sollberger discussed the children of the Ur HI kings and listed
as many as “‘54 princes et princesses” under the “descendance de
Sulgir” (= Sulgi), among them at least 18 children of Sulgi and at
least 18 children of Amar-Sin (= Bar-Sin), including 12 sons ''*.

Scholars, who must have noticed it, have been loath to comment
upon the great imbalance between a single royal wife and as many
as 18-20 children. As I see it, the two pertinent questions that should
be considered are the matter of secondary wives and the exact meaning
of dumu lugal and dumu-sAl lugal.

The first and most immediate interpretation is to assume that, beside
a reigning wife, the rulers of the Ur Ill dynasty had several con-
cubines'!, and all the many children of a king were the result of

 

 

his union with the reigning wife and other ladies. he other possibility

is not to take seriously the translation of dumu lugal as “the son
of the king” and of dumu-SAL lugal as “the daughter of the king”
and to look for a different interpretation.

Munich in 1970 I made a statement that the meaning of dumu lugal
(and, similarly, dumu-sAL lugal) is not necessarily limited to the
sons (and daughters) of the reigning king but that it encompasses

pretation on the basis of my experience with the meaning “sons of
the king” in the hieroglyphic Hittite texts. Indirect evidence in favor
of that assumption is found among the Hittites and Egyptians with
their extraordinary number of persons called “son of the king” or
“daughter of the king”. One pregnant example from the annals of
the Hittite king MurSili8 shows that a person called DUMU.LUGAL,

Bettina Schmitz dedicated an extensive monograph to the study of
the title “king’s son” and “king’s daughter” among the Egyptians '??.
The situation varies greatly from period to period, but what is
important is that, in varying situations, these titles may be applied
not only to the king’s real sons and daughters '?3, but also to other

title was bestowed '*’. Unfortunately, I know of no comparable

The conclusion that can be drawn about the family of the two non-
royal votants (section 7.2.2) and of the royal family is that each con-
tained a larger number of children than posited for the families of
average- and low-status individuals in the sources a) to f), treated on
p. 60-65. This applies, of course, also to the Ur HI royal families,
since the phrases “‘sons of the king” and “daughters of the king”
should denote, in a majority of cases, the children of the reigning king.

7.2.4. Sale Contracts

Nothing in the sources treated heretofore indicates anything but
a nuclear type of family for average individuals, persons of higher
status, and royalty.

The existence of the extended type of family in early Mesopotamian
times up to and including the Sargonic period can be proved by the
analysis of the sale contracts on clay, which deal with various kinds
of property, such as land, houses, orchards, slaves. and animals, and
of the ancient kudurrus, which deal exclusively with land.

As can be seen from the charts (to be published in the kudurru
volume), giving a synopsis of all the sale contracts from the Fara,
Pre-Sargonic, Sargonic, and Ur HII periods, surprising results can be
obtained in respect to the number of sellers belonging to one kinship
grouping, as it varies from large to small between the Fara and Ur Ill
periods.
